questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.text: What is the first action before assessing an adult who may need CPR?

answers.text: Verify that the scene is safe
Check the carotid pulse immediately
Apply AED pads before checking the area
Move the person before looking for hazards

explanations.a: The rescuer should first make sure the scene is safe before approaching and starting assessment. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Pulse checking comes after scene safety and responsiveness assessment.
explanations.c: AED use should not begin until the rescuer can safely approach.
explanations.d: Answer boundary: the person should not be moved unless the environment is unsafe or CPR cannot be performed effectively.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.text: How should a rescuer check responsiveness in an adult?

answers.text: Shake the person aggressively by the neck
Tap the shoulders and shout to see if the person responds
Check only for eye color changes
Give water and wait for swallowing

explanations.a: Rough movement can cause injury and is not the recommended responsiveness check.
explanations.b: Adult BLS assessment includes tapping the shoulders and shouting to check responsiveness. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Eye color is not a responsiveness assessment step.
explanations.d: Giving water can delay care and may be unsafe for an unresponsive person.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.text: During adult BLS assessment, which finding means the rescuer should call for help and continue the BLS assessment?

answers.text: The rescuer has gloves available
The person answers clearly and asks for privacy
The person is unresponsive after tapping and shouting
The scene contains no hazards

explanations.a: PPE supports safety, but it is not the patient response finding.
explanations.b: A responsive person needs assessment, but this does not match cardiac arrest recognition.
explanations.c: Unresponsiveness is a key finding that triggers help, emergency response activation, and further assessment. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: A safe scene permits assessment but does not by itself show the person needs CPR.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.text: Why does the scene safety check come before touching the person?

answers.text: It confirms whether an AED shock is needed
It replaces the need for checking breathing
It determines the person's age category
A rescuer who becomes injured may not be able to help

explanations.a: AED shock decisions occur after rhythm analysis by the AED.
explanations.b: Breathing assessment is still needed after scene safety and responsiveness.
explanations.c: Answer boundary: age category is not the purpose of scene safety.
explanations.d: Scene safety protects the rescuer, bystanders, and the person needing care. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.text: Which finding means the rescuer should call for help and continue the BLS assessment?

answers.text: The person answers clearly and asks for privacy (per AHA technique)
The scene contains no hazards (per AHA technique)
The person is unresponsive after tapping and shouting (per AHA technique)
The rescuer has gloves available (per AHA technique)

explanations.a: A responsive person needs assessment, but this does not match cardiac arrest recognition.
explanations.b: Answer boundary: a safe scene permits assessment but does not by itself show the person needs CPR.
explanations.c: Unresponsiveness is a key finding that triggers help, emergency response activation, and further assessment. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: PPE supports safety, but it is not the patient response finding.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.keyword: emergency response activation and AED retrieval
questions.text: When should the AED be used during suspected cardiac arrest?

answers.text: Solely if a pulse is strong and breathing is normal
Solely after EMS arrives with permission
Solely after 10 minutes of CPR
As soon as it is available

explanations.a: AED use is for suspected cardiac arrest, not normal circulation.
explanations.b: Trained responders and lay rescuers should use an AED promptly when available.
explanations.c: Delaying AED use can reduce survival chances.
explanations.d: The adult BLS sequence uses the AED as soon as it arrives and is available. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.keyword: emergency response activation and AED retrieval
questions.text: A rescuer is assessing an unresponsive adult. What should a rescuer do when an adult is unresponsive?

answers.text: Shout for nearby help and activate the emergency response system
Give repeated breaths before calling for help
Wait until CPR has been done for several minutes
Leave the person alone without calling anyone

explanations.a: An unresponsive adult should trigger help, emergency response activation, and AED retrieval. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Help and AED retrieval should not be delayed.
explanations.c: Emergency response should be activated early.
explanations.d: Leaving without activating help delays lifesaving care.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.keyword: emergency response activation and AED retrieval
questions.text: If another person is nearby, what should the rescuer ask them to do?

answers.text: Search for paperwork before calling
Activate emergency response and get the AED
Hold the person's arms down during assessment
Wait quietly until the rescuer finishes all assessment steps

explanations.a: Answer boundary: paperwork does not take priority over emergency response.
explanations.b: The BLS sequence includes sending someone to call for help and bring the AED. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Restraining the person is not the needed emergency action.
explanations.d: A second person can activate help and retrieve the AED immediately.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.keyword: emergency response activation and AED retrieval
questions.text: Why is early AED retrieval important?

answers.text: The AED replaces checking responsiveness
The AED should be used only after normal breathing returns
Defibrillation may be needed for shockable cardiac arrest rhythms
The AED gives rescue breaths automatically

explanations.a: The rescuer still checks responsiveness and breathing or pulse.
explanations.b: AED use is for suspected cardiac arrest, not delayed until recovery.
explanations.c: AED availability is time-critical because shockable rhythms need early defibrillation. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: AEDs analyze rhythms and deliver shocks when indicated; they do not ventilate the person.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.keyword: emergency response activation and AED retrieval
questions.text: During adult BLS assessment, what should a rescuer do when an adult is unresponsive?

answers.text: Shout for nearby help and activate the emergency response system (per AHA technique)
Wait until CPR has been done for several minutes (per AHA technique)
Leave the person alone without calling anyone (per AHA technique)
Give repeated breaths before calling for help (per AHA technique)

explanations.a: An unresponsive adult should trigger help, emergency response activation, and AED retrieval. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Emergency response should be activated early.
explanations.c: Leaving without activating help delays lifesaving care.
explanations.d: Help and AED retrieval should not be delayed.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: How is the adult carotid pulse located?

answers.text: Use the thumb on the wrist
Place 2 or 3 fingers on the trachea and slide into the groove between the trachea and neck muscles
Place a palm over the center of the chest
Press both sides of the neck hard at the same time

explanations.a: The wrist pulse is not the adult BLS carotid check.
explanations.b: The carotid pulse is found by sliding into the groove beside the trachea. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: The chest is not where the carotid pulse is checked.
explanations.d: Pressing both sides can impair blood flow and is not the taught method.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: What should the rescuer look for while checking breathing?

answers.text: Whether the person has jewelry
Whether the person is wearing shoes
Normal breathing or absence of normal breathing, including gasping
Whether the person can blink on command without being addressed

explanations.a: Jewelry is unrelated to breathing assessment unless it interferes later with AED pads.
explanations.b: Shoes do not determine breathing status.
explanations.c: The assessment distinguishes normal breathing from no breathing or only gasping. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: The BLS breathing check focuses on breathing movement and quality.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: How should breathing and pulse be checked in adult BLS?

answers.text: One at a time for 30 seconds each
Solely after the AED analyzes rhythm
Solely after rescue breaths have been given
At the same time

explanations.a: Separate long checks delay compressions.
explanations.b: Assessment begins before AED rhythm analysis.
explanations.c: Breathing and pulse assessment determines whether CPR or rescue breathing is needed.
explanations.d: Breathing and pulse are assessed simultaneously to reduce delay in starting CPR. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: How long should the breathing and pulse check take?

answers.text: At least 5 seconds and no more than 10 seconds
Exactly 30 seconds
Until the rescuer feels completely certain, regardless of time
Less than 1 second

explanations.a: The check should last at least 5 seconds but not exceed 10 seconds. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: A 30-second check delays CPR.
explanations.c: The time limit prevents harmful delays.
explanations.d: A check that short may miss breathing or pulse findings.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: Which pulse is checked for an adult during BLS assessment?

answers.text: Temporal pulse
Carotid pulse
Brachial pulse
Pedal pulse

explanations.a: A temporal pulse is not used for adult BLS cardiac arrest assessment.
explanations.b: Adult BLS uses the carotid pulse during the breathing and pulse check. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Brachial pulse checks are used for infants, not adult assessment.
explanations.d: A pedal pulse is not the standard adult BLS pulse check.

questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time

answers.text: Press both sides of the neck hard at the same time (per AHA technique)
Use the thumb on the wrist (per AHA technique)
Place 2 or 3 fingers on the trachea and slide into the groove between the trachea and neck muscles (per AHA technique)
Place a palm over the center of the chest (per AHA technique)

explanations.a: Pressing both sides can impair blood flow and is not the taught method.
explanations.b: The wrist pulse is not the adult BLS carotid check.

explanations.d: The chest is not where the carotid pulse is checked.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.4 Recognize cardiac arrest signs including agonal gasps and seizure-like activity
questions.text: Which sounds may be associated with agonal gasps?

answers.text: Clear speech and full sentences
Gasping, snorting, snoring, or groaning
A steady normal breathing pattern
Normal coughing after drinking water

explanations.a: Clear speech is responsiveness, not agonal gasping.
explanations.b: Agonal gasps may sound like gasping, snorting, snoring, or groaning. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Agonal gasps are abnormal, not steady normal breathing.
explanations.d: The scenario is not the same as agonal gasping in cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.4 Recognize cardiac arrest signs including agonal gasps and seizure-like activity
questions.text: During adult BLS assessment, what can seizure-like activity during the first minutes after collapse indicate?

answers.text: The AED must not be used under any circumstances
CPR assessment should be delayed until all movement stops
Possible cardiac arrest
The person definitely has normal circulation

explanations.a: AED use may still be needed if cardiac arrest is present.
explanations.b: Assessment should continue promptly.
explanations.c: Seizure-like activity can happen early in cardiac arrest and should not prevent cardiac arrest assessment. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: Seizure-like movement does not rule out cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.4 Recognize cardiac arrest signs including agonal gasps and seizure-like activity
questions.text: Which combination indicates cardiac arrest in adult BLS?

answers.text: A pulse with abnormal breathing
Normal breathing and a definite pulse
Responsive speech with normal breathing
No normal breathing and no definite pulse

explanations.a: A pulse with abnormal breathing calls for rescue breathing and monitoring, not immediate compressions unless the pulse is lost.
explanations.b: Normal breathing with a pulse is not cardiac arrest.
explanations.c: Answer boundary: a responsive person with normal breathing does not need CPR.
explanations.d: No normal breathing or only gasping with no definite pulse is treated as cardiac arrest. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.4 Recognize cardiac arrest signs including agonal gasps and seizure-like activity
questions.text: How should agonal gasps be treated during assessment?

answers.text: As not normal breathing
As normal breathing that means CPR is unnecessary
As a reason to give water
As proof that a pulse is present

explanations.a: Agonal gasps are not normal breathing and should be treated as a sign of cardiac arrest. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Agonal gasps can occur during cardiac arrest and should not delay CPR.
explanations.c: Water is unsafe for an unresponsive person and delays care.
explanations.d: Gasping does not prove circulation is adequate.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.4 Recognize cardiac arrest signs including agonal gasps and seizure-like activity
questions.text: What can seizure-like activity during the first minutes after collapse indicate?

answers.text: CPR assessment should be delayed until all movement stops (per AHA technique)
The person definitely has normal circulation (per AHA technique)
Possible cardiac arrest (per AHA technique)
The AED must not be used under any circumstances (per AHA technique)

explanations.a: Assessment should continue promptly.
explanations.b: Answer boundary: seizure-like movement does not rule out cardiac arrest.
explanations.c: Seizure-like activity can happen early in cardiac arrest and should not prevent cardiac arrest assessment. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: AED use may still be needed if cardiac arrest is present.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.text: During training, a rescuer is assessing an unresponsive adult. What should the rescuer do if a pulse is uncertain after no more than 10 seconds?

answers.text: Start CPR
Delay care until a second rescuer confirms the pulse
Use the AED only and avoid compressions
Assume the pulse is present because checking is difficult

explanations.a: If the rescuer does not definitely feel a pulse within 10 seconds, CPR should begin. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Waiting for confirmation can delay lifesaving compressions.
explanations.c: AED use is important, but compressions should begin when no pulse is definite.
explanations.d: Uncertainty should not delay CPR when cardiac arrest is possible.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.text: If opioid overdose is suspected and naloxone is available, what action may be included?

answers.text: Use naloxone only after the person is fully recovered
Administer an opioid antagonist while continuing standard BLS care
Use naloxone instead of activating emergency response
Delay breathing support until naloxone works

explanations.a: Answer boundary: naloxone is used during suspected opioid-associated emergencies, not after recovery only.
explanations.b: The adult sequence includes giving an opioid antagonist if available when overdose is suspected. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Naloxone does not replace EMS activation or BLS care.
explanations.d: Ventilation and CPR decisions should not be delayed.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.text: If an adult has a pulse but is not breathing normally, what should the rescuer do?

answers.text: Start chest compressions immediately without breaths
Wait without giving breaths until EMS arrives
Give 1 breath every 6 seconds
Give 30 compressions before checking breathing again

explanations.a: Compressions are started when no pulse is definitely felt.
explanations.b: Rescue breathing supports oxygenation while a pulse is present.
explanations.c: With a pulse but absent or abnormal breathing, give 1 breath every 6 seconds, or 10 breaths per minute. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: The assessment shows a pulse is present, so rescue breathing is the initial response.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.text: How often should the pulse be rechecked when giving rescue breaths to an adult with a pulse?

answers.text: Every 10 minutes
Solely after the AED shocks
Every 10 seconds
Every 2 minutes

explanations.a: Waiting too long may delay CPR if the pulse is lost.
explanations.b: Pulse reassessment is needed during rescue breathing even before any AED shock.
explanations.c: Very frequent checks interrupt ventilation and care.
explanations.d: The rescuer should recheck the pulse every 2 minutes while giving rescue breaths. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.text: During adult BLS assessment, If an adult is not breathing or only gasping and no pulse is felt, what should the rescuer do?

answers.text: Start CPR beginning with chest compressions
Wait for the person to breathe normally
Give water and place the person upright
Continue checking the pulse for 1 minute

explanations.a: No normal breathing and no definite pulse means start CPR with compressions. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Waiting can reduce the chance of survival.
explanations.c: Food or fluids are unsafe and delay CPR.
explanations.d: Pulse checks longer than 10 seconds delay compressions.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.text: What should the rescuer do if a pulse is uncertain after no more than 10 seconds?

answers.text: Assume the pulse is present because checking is difficult (per AHA technique)
Start CPR (per AHA technique)
Delay care until a second rescuer confirms the pulse (per AHA technique)
Use the AED only and avoid compressions (per AHA technique)

explanations.a: Uncertainty should not delay CPR when cardiac arrest is possible.
explanations.b: If the rescuer does not definitely feel a pulse within 10 seconds, CPR should begin. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Waiting for confirmation can delay lifesaving compressions.
explanations.d: AED use is important, but compressions should begin when no pulse is definite.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.text: A bystander responds to a person who has collapsed inside a coffee shop. According to AHA Part 2, what defines an adequate responsiveness check before starting CPR?

answers.text: Tap both shoulders firmly while shouting "Are you okay?" and look for any movement or response
Lift the eyelids and shine a flashlight to test pupil reaction
Pinch the cheek and time the response with a stopwatch
Squeeze the chest forcefully to elicit a withdrawal reflex

explanations.a: AHA Part 2: tap shoulders firmly and shout — verbal and tactile stimulation, looking for any response or movement.
explanations.b: Pupil testing is part of advanced assessment, not the lay-rescuer responsiveness check.
explanations.c: Pinching the cheek with timing is not part of the AHA protocol.
explanations.d: Forceful chest squeezing risks injury and is not the recommended check.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.text: After confirming an unresponsive adult is not breathing normally, a single rescuer is alone in a small office. According to AHA Part 2, what is the correct action regarding the AED and EMS?

answers.text: Begin compressions for 2 minutes before doing anything else
Activate the emergency response system (call 911) and request someone to bring an AED if available; if alone, use a phone speaker to keep 911 on the line and continue care
Wait until 5 cycles of CPR are complete before calling 911
Skip the AED step entirely if not visible

explanations.a: Adult collapse with sudden onset is presumed cardiac and benefits most from rapid defibrillation; do not delay the call.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: activate emergency response immediately for adult sudden collapse; use phone speaker if alone so dispatcher can guide care while CPR continues.
explanations.c: Delaying the 911 call delays defibrillation; 911 is called as part of the recognition phase, not after CPR.
explanations.d: AED use is encouraged whenever an AED is available; "not visible" is not an acceptable reason to skip the request.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: A trained rescuer is performing the simultaneous breathing/pulse check on an unresponsive adult. According to AHA Part 2, how long should this combined check take?

answers.text: No more than 10 seconds — if pulse and normal breathing are not clearly present within that time, begin CPR
At least 30 seconds to be sure of the absence of pulse
Exactly 60 seconds to count beats accurately
As long as needed; there is no time limit on the pulse check

explanations.a: AHA Part 2: simultaneous check ≤10 seconds; if no definite pulse and no normal breathing, begin compressions — long pulse checks delay treatment.
explanations.b: 30 seconds far exceeds the AHA limit and delays compressions.
explanations.c: A 60-second count is unnecessarily long and incorrectly assumes pulse rate matters more than presence.
explanations.d: AHA explicitly limits pulse checks to ≤10 seconds to prevent delayed CPR.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.4 Recognize cardiac arrest signs including agonal gasps and seizure-like activity
questions.keyword: agonal gasps not normal breathing arrest
questions.text: A bystander watches an adult collapse and notes the person is making slow, infrequent gasping sounds. According to AHA Part 2, what do these gasps indicate?

answers.text: Normal sleep breathing — no intervention needed
A sign of returning consciousness
Voluntary attempts to clear the throat
Agonal gasping — irregular, gasping breaths during cardiac arrest that should NOT be mistaken for normal breathing; treat the patient as in arrest and begin CPR

explanations.a: Agonal gasps are abnormal — they are not sleep breathing.
explanations.b: Agonal gasps indicate ongoing brainstem activity in arrest, not recovery.
explanations.c: They are involuntary; the patient is unconscious.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2: agonal gasps are a hallmark of cardiac arrest in the early minutes; do not treat them as normal breathing — start CPR.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.keyword: rescue breathing only pulse present 1 breath 6 seconds
questions.text: During the assessment of an unresponsive adult, a trained rescuer detects a definite pulse but no breathing or only abnormal/agonal gasping. According to AHA Part 2, what is the appropriate action?

answers.text: Begin full CPR with chest compressions and rescue breaths immediately
Provide rescue breathing only — 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min for adults) — and reassess pulse every 2 minutes
Place in the recovery position and observe
Wait for return of spontaneous breathing without intervention

explanations.a: Compressions are not indicated when a pulse is present; rescue breathing alone is the right intervention.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: pulse present + no breathing = rescue breathing alone; for adults, 1 breath every 6 seconds (about 10/min). Reassess pulse every ~2 minutes.
explanations.c: Recovery position is for breathing patients; an apneic patient needs assisted ventilation.
explanations.d: Waiting for spontaneous breathing while the patient is apneic risks rapid hypoxic deterioration.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.1 Verify scene safety and check responsiveness
questions.keyword: electrical hazard scene safety power off
questions.text: A rescuer arrives at a scene where the patient is on a wet pool deck and another bystander has been "shocked" by an exposed wire. According to AHA Part 2, what is the FIRST priority?

answers.text: Begin compressions on the patient regardless of the surroundings
Move the patient yourself before any other action even if the area is still energized
Reach the patient quickly and risk a second casualty
Ensure scene safety by removing the electrical hazard (have power disconnected) before approaching the patient — a rescuer who becomes a casualty cannot help

explanations.a: Beginning compressions in a still-hazardous area risks rescuer electrocution and a second arrest.
explanations.b: Moving the patient through an energized area transfers the hazard.
explanations.c: Multiplying casualties is the explicit failure mode AHA scene safety guidance prevents.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2: scene safety is the first BLS step; eliminate the hazard (turn off power, remove dangling wires) before approaching, especially in electrical/water emergencies.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.2 Activate emergency response and get the AED
questions.keyword: remote rural EMS poor coverage adaptation
questions.text: In a remote rural area with poor cell coverage, a single rescuer finds an unresponsive adult in arrest. According to AHA Part 2, what is the appropriate adaptation?

answers.text: Skip activating EMS entirely — coverage is poor anyway
Drive the patient to the nearest hospital before any CPR
Wait for someone with a satellite phone to arrive

Try every method to reach EMS (cell, landline, two-way radio, runner to a building with phone) while continuing CPR; if alone with no contact, perform 2 minutes of CPR before leaving briefly to seek help if needed (per pediatric/asphyxial logic if young patient)

explanations.a: Skipping EMS abandons the patient; alternative communication routes should be explored.
explanations.b: Driving an arrest victim alone is unsafe and stops CPR; CPR continues during transport only with help.
explanations.c: Passive waiting risks death; actively continue CPR while seeking communication.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2 recognizes resource-limited settings: continue CPR, attempt every available communication channel, and adapt the standard "phone first, push first, breathe first" sequence to circumstances.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.3 Assess breathing and pulse at the same time
questions.text: A trained rescuer assessing an unresponsive adult is unsure whether they feel a pulse — palpation is ambiguous. According to AHA Part 2, what should the rescuer do?

answers.text: Spend an additional 30 seconds attempting to clarify the pulse before any action
Default to assuming a pulse is present and provide rescue breathing only

When in doubt about pulse, treat the patient as in cardiac arrest and begin compressions — delayed compressions cause harm; unnecessary compressions on a perfusing patient cause minimal harm in this acute setting
Wait for a more experienced rescuer before doing anything

explanations.a: Extending pulse checks beyond 10 seconds is explicitly discouraged.
explanations.b: Defaulting to assumed pulse risks delaying needed compressions; AHA defaults the other way.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2: when uncertain about pulse in an unresponsive non-breathing adult, begin chest compressions — the cost of delayed CPR exceeds the cost of brief unnecessary compressions.
explanations.d: Waiting for a more experienced rescuer abandons time-sensitive care.

questions.name: Assessment and Recognition
questions.objective: 2.5 Identify response actions when pulse or breathing findings differ
questions.keyword: ROSC perfusing rhythm stop compressions support ventilation
questions.text: During CPR on an adult, the rescuer team performs a 10-second rhythm check after 2 minutes. The rescuer detects a faint pulse and gasping breaths. According to AHA Part 2 / Part 4, what is the next action?

answers.text: Continue compressions and breaths at full intensity to be safe
Stop all care and let the patient rest
Compress at a slower rate to "ease into" recovery
Stop compressions, support ventilation as needed (rescue breathing if breaths are inadequate), monitor closely, and reassess every 2 minutes — perfusing rhythm requires no compressions

explanations.a: Compressing on a perfusing patient with returning circulation is not indicated.
explanations.b: Stopping all care misses needed ventilation support during the early ROSC phase.
explanations.c: Compression rate is set by AHA at 100–120/min when compressions are indicated; "easing" is not a parameter.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2 / Part 4: when ROSC achieves a perfusing rhythm during CPR, stop compressions, support ventilation as needed, and monitor; reassess regularly.
